findings.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:185 — P1/100: `work_queue: queue.Queue[WorkItem[T]] = queue.Queue()` gives every worker an unbounded queue, so sustained Kafka input above database-processing capacity materializes both payloads and decoded results until OOM; bounded Kafka polls do not rebut this because repeated `submit` calls never observe downstream capacity and `poll()` only emits a metric.

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:148 — P1/100: `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset)` runs in `finally` and therefore transitions failed processing to the same completed state as successful processing, allowing the commit loop to advance past a result that was never applied.

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/result_consumer.py:133 — P1/75: `self.queue_pool = FixedQueuePool(` makes a partition-assignment strategy consume a factory-owned shared pool that its own `close()` permanently shuts down, so the next `create_with_partitions` after rebalance reuses dead queues and cannot process the new assignment; final factory cleanup does not rebut this because assignment strategies close while the factory remains reusable.

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:336 — P1/100: `self.shutdown_event.set()` stops the sole commit loop before `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` handles in-flight and queued work, while that shutdown first sets `worker.shutdown = True`, so graceful close abandons queued results and leaves results finishing during close without any path to commit their offsets.

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/result_consumer.py:136 — P1/100: `num_queues=max_workers or 20` fails to enforce the positive-worker invariant, so a negative parsed `--max-workers` creates zero queues and every message is rejected before the catch path marks its offset complete, committing an entirely unprocessed stream.

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:83 — P2/100: `min_offset = min(all_offsets)` and `max_offset = max(all_offsets)` rescan an ever-growing per-partition set on every commit tick and then linearly walk the range, so one slow earliest offset under sustained ingress produces unbounded offset materialization and cumulative quadratic work; the one-second cadence limits call frequency but not the growing cost of every call.

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:202 — P2/100: `return hash(group_key) % self.num_queues` maps unrelated subscriptions onto one single-threaded FIFO, so any hot or slow subscription head-of-line blocks every colliding subscription and collapses usable parallelism; uniform hashing balances key counts but cannot balance per-key work or remove deterministic collisions.

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:31 — P2/100: `message: Message[KafkaPayload | FilteredPayload]` is never read after construction, so deleting this field and its constructor argument changes no behavior while preventing every unbounded backlog entry from retaining the original encoded Kafka payload alongside its decoded result; future offset access does not justify the coupling because `partition` and `offset` are already stored explicitly.

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:344 — P2/100: `def join(self, timeout: float | None = None) -> None: self.close()` ignores the `ProcessingStrategy.join` timeout contract and starts shutdown again, so a caller requesting a bounded join can instead wait through the commit-thread timeout plus up to five seconds for each worker.

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:233 — P1/100: `worker.shutdown = True` makes every worker exit after its current item before `shutdown(immediate=False)` can drain the queue, so a normal graceful close abandons all remaining uptime results despite the stated no-loss guarantee.

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:338 — P1/75: `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` destroys the factory-owned pool whenever an assignment strategy closes, so the next strategy created after a Kafka rebalance reuses queues with no live workers and cannot process its assigned messages.

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:185 — P1/100: `work_queue: queue.Queue[WorkItem[T]] = queue.Queue()` creates an unbounded queue per worker, so sustained input above processing capacity grows memory without limit instead of supplying the documented natural backpressure.

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/result_consumer.py:136 — P2/100: `num_queues=max_workers or 20` accepts a negative `--max-workers` as a negative queue count and silently converts zero to 20, so validly parsed CLI inputs either create no usable workers or violate the requested parallelism limit.

tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py:1820 — P2/100: `assert mock_processor_call.call_count == 2` only proves both subscription callbacks eventually ran and passes when they run serially, leaving the feature's core cross-subscription parallelism requirement entirely unverified.

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:149 — P1/100: `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset)` runs in `finally` after `except Exception:`, so every failed result callback becomes committable and is permanently skipped after restart; the strongest counterargument is that poison records must not stall the partition, but it fails because transient database and downstream failures are treated identically and no dead-letter or replay copy preserves the source record.

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:323 — P1/100: `self.queue_pool.offset_tracker.complete_offset(` unconditionally marks a record successful after any decode, grouping, or queue-submission exception, so schema-skewed records during rollout and records rejected by a closed pool are committed without processing; the strongest counterargument is that broad exception handling keeps consumption live, but it fails because liveness is purchased by irreversible silent loss with no quarantine or backfill source.

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:338 — P1/75: `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` permanently closes the factory-owned shared pool when Arroyo closes one partition-assignment strategy, so the next `create_with_partitions` after a rebalance reuses shut queues whose rejected submissions are caught and marked complete without processing.

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:336 — P2/100: `self.shutdown_event.set()` stops the only commit loop before `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` waits for active workers, so work that finishes during close can never reach the commit callback and is replayed after restart.

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:234 — P2/100: `worker.shutdown = True` is set before non-immediate queue shutdown, so each worker exits after at most its current item and leaves all remaining queued messages abandoned instead of draining them during the advertised graceful shutdown.

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:149 — P1/100: `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset)` runs in `finally` after `except Exception:`, so a transient database or downstream failure is swallowed and its Kafka record becomes committable without being applied; skipping poison records is the strongest counterargument, but it fails because this catch treats retryable operational failures identically and preserves no replay or quarantine copy.

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:323 — P1/100: `self.queue_pool.offset_tracker.complete_offset(` marks a record complete after any decode, grouping, hashing, or queue-submission exception, so the commit loop permanently advances past work that never entered a worker; keeping the consumer live is the strongest counterargument, but it fails because logging alone cannot recover an already committed source record.

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:301 — P1/100: `if result is None:` followed by `complete_offset(partition, offset)` converts the decoder's catch-all failure return into successful completion, so transient codec failures silently discard payloads; intentionally skipping `FilteredPayload` is the strongest counterargument, but it fails because `decode_payload` returns the same `None` for every unexpected decoding exception.

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:336 — P1/100: `self.shutdown_event.set()` stops the sole commit loop before `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` sets every `worker.shutdown = True`, so graceful close abandons queued results and returns while results finishing after the final commit snapshot remain uncommitted and replay; eventual Kafka replay is the strongest counterargument, but it fails because the advertised graceful operation is partial and re-executes side effects already completed during shutdown.

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/result_consumer.py:133 — P1/75: `self.queue_pool = FixedQueuePool(` creates one factory-owned pool while each assignment strategy executes `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` in `close()`, so the next `create_with_partitions` after a rebalance reuses shut queues whose rejected submissions are caught and committed as complete; final factory cleanup is the strongest counterargument, but it fails because assignment strategies close during rebalances while the factory remains reusable.

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:185 — P1/100: `work_queue: queue.Queue[WorkItem[T]] = queue.Queue()` gives every worker an unbounded queue, so Kafka input above processing capacity grows retained payloads and decoded results until OOM instead of applying backpressure; bounded Kafka polling is the strongest counterargument, but it fails because every `submit()` returns immediately regardless of downstream backlog.

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/result_consumer.py:136 — P1/100: `num_queues=max_workers or 20` accepts a negative parsed `--max-workers`, constructs zero queues, and causes every submission to raise before the broad catch marks its offset complete, silently committing the entire unprocessed stream; invalid operator input is the strongest counterargument, but it fails because the CLI accepts the value and the runtime reports successful consumption instead of rejecting startup.

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:281 — P3/100: `metrics.incr("remote_subscriptions.queue_pool.offsets_committed",` executes before `self.commit_function(committable)`, so every failed commit is reported as committed and the same offsets inflate the success counter on each retry; eventual retry success is the strongest counterargument, but it fails because monitoring lies throughout the outage and overcounts the final successful offsets.

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:185 — P2, confidence 75: `work_queue: queue.Queue[WorkItem[T]] = queue.Queue()` creates an unbounded per-worker queue, so a result flood or hot subscription that lets Kafka delivery outpace processing grows resident memory until the uptime consumer is killed and results stop being processed; Kafka-side pacing is the strongest counterargument, but it does not survive because `submit()` has no capacity check or blocking boundary and `Queue`'s default `maxsize=0` never backpressures.

tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py:1922 — (P1, confidence 100) `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` samples state only 0.2 seconds after work finishes even though the commit loop runs once per second, so it passes while the failed offset is marked complete and later committed, causing message loss; the strongest counterargument is that the test only needs to prove the second message runs, but its claimed error-handling contract is specifically about commits and the assertion never observes the commit interval.

tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py:2005 — (P1, confidence 100) `assert factory.queue_pool is None` proves only that a reference was cleared, so the graceful-shutdown test passes when queued results are dropped or the strategy's commit thread remains alive; the strongest counterargument is that `shutdown()` joins workers, but the assertion never verifies all five submitted results were processed or that the strategy thread terminated.

tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py:1820 — (P2, confidence 100) `assert mock_processor_call.call_count == 2` proves completion rather than concurrency, so a fully serial implementation or two subscription IDs hashing to the same queue passes and the parallelism feature can regress undetected; the strongest counterargument is that two workers were configured, but no barrier, overlap interval, or worker identity is asserted.

tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py:200 — (P3, confidence 100) `assert stats["total_items"] > 0` races live workers running a trivial processor and fails whenever they drain all ten queues before the snapshot; the strongest counterargument is that ten submissions usually create a backlog, but queue size excludes in-flight work and scheduling can deterministically make the observed total zero.

tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py:106 — (P3, confidence 100) `assert len(queue_indices) == 3` assumes salted Python hashes for twenty fixed strings occupy every bucket and fails under `PYTHONHASHSEED=211`, where they occupy only two; the strongest counterargument is that twenty samples make full coverage likely, but randomized test-process seeds turn that probability into reproducible CI flakiness.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:185 — P1/100: `work_queue: queue.Queue[WorkItem[T]] = queue.Queue()` gives every worker an unbounded queue, so sustained Kafka input above database-processing capacity materializes both payloads and decoded results until OOM; bounded Kafka polls do not rebut this because repeated `submit` calls never observe downstream capacity and `poll()` only emits a metric.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `work_queue: queue.Queue[WorkItem[T]] = queue.Queue()` at line 185 creates unbounded queues. The `submit` method in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` (lines 289-316) calls `self.queue_pool.submit()` which puts items into these unbounded queues without any backpressure mechanism. The `poll()` method only emits metrics and doesn't provide flow control. If Kafka produces messages faster than workers can process them (e.g., slow database operations), items will accumulate indefinitely in memory. This is a real memory exhaustion bug - the queues have no maxsize parameter, so they grow unbounded.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:148 — P1/100: `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset)` runs in `finally` and therefore transitions failed processing to the same completed state as successful processing, allowing the commit loop to advance past a result that was never applied.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that in OrderedQueueWorker.run() at line 148, the `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset)` is in a `finally` block. Looking at the code structure (lines 127-148), when an exception occurs during `self.result_processor(self.identifier, work_item.result)`, the exception is caught and logged (lines 140-143), but the `finally` block still executes `complete_offset`. This means failed processing is marked as complete, allowing the commit loop to advance past messages that failed to process. The commit loop in `_commit_loop` (lines 262-280) will then commit these offsets, potentially losing data. This is a real correctness bug - failed messages should not be marked as successfully processed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/result_consumer.py:133 — P1/75: `self.queue_pool = FixedQueuePool(` makes a partition-assignment strategy consume a factory-owned shared pool that its own `close()` permanently shuts down, so the next `create_with_partitions` after rebalance reuses dead queues and cannot process the new assignment; final factory cleanup does not rebut this because assignment strategies close while the factory remains reusable.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real issue: In result_consumer.py, the FixedQueuePool is created once in __init__ (line 133) and stored as factory.queue_pool. When create_thread_queue_parallel_worker is called, it creates a SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy that references this pool. When that strategy's close() method is called (e.g., during rebalance), it calls self.queue_pool.shutdown() which sets worker.shutdown=True and calls q.shutdown() on all queues. The factory's shutdown() method also sets self.queue_pool = None. However, if the factory is reused after a rebalance (create_with_partitions called again), the queue_pool would either be None or have dead workers. Looking at the code flow: factory.__init__ creates queue_pool -> create_with_partitions -> create_thread_queue_parallel_worker uses queue_pool -> strategy.close() shuts down pool -> next create_with_partitions would fail because queue_pool workers are dead. This is a legitimate lifecycle bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:336 — P1/100: `self.shutdown_event.set()` stops the sole commit loop before `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` handles in-flight and queued work, while that shutdown first sets `worker.shutdown = True`, so graceful close abandons queued results and leaves results finishing during close without any path to commit their offsets.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a race condition in the close() method. Looking at lines 335-338, close() sets shutdown_event which stops the commit_loop thread, then calls queue_pool.shutdown(). The commit_loop (lines 275-293) is responsible for committing offsets. When shutdown_event is set, the commit_loop exits its while loop and stops committing. Meanwhile, queue_pool.shutdown() (lines 227-237) sets worker.shutdown=True and calls q.shutdown(), but workers may still be processing items. Any offsets completed after the commit_loop exits will never be committed. This is a real ordering bug - the commit loop should continue running until all workers finish processing, not be stopped first.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/result_consumer.py:136 — P1/100: `num_queues=max_workers or 20` fails to enforce the positive-worker invariant, so a negative parsed `--max-workers` creates zero queues and every message is rejected before the catch path marks its offset complete, committing an entirely unprocessed stream.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that a negative --max-workers would create zero queues. However, looking at the diff: 1) The click.Option for max_workers has type=int with default=None, but there's no validation preventing negative values at the CLI level. 2) The code uses `num_queues=max_workers or 20`, which means if max_workers is None or 0, it defaults to 20. A negative number like -1 is truthy in Python, so it would be used. 3) However, FixedQueuePool with num_queues=-1 would create an empty range(num_queues) loop, creating 0 queues and 0 workers. But the finding's claim about 'every message is rejected before the catch path marks its offset complete' is not accurate - looking at submit() in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy, messages go through decoder and then queue_pool.submit(). With 0 queues, get_queue_for_group would return hash % 0 which raises ZeroDivisionError, not silent rejection. The scenario is contrived (negative CLI args) and the described failure mode is inaccurate.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:83 — P2/100: `min_offset = min(all_offsets)` and `max_offset = max(all_offsets)` rescan an ever-growing per-partition set on every commit tick and then linearly walk the range, so one slow earliest offset under sustained ingress produces unbounded offset materialization and cumulative quadratic work; the one-second cadence limits call frequency but not the growing cost of every call.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a performance concern in the OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets() method. Looking at lines 75-97 of queue_consumer.py, the code does: (1) call min(all_offsets) and max(all_offsets) which scan the entire set, (2) iterate through range(start, max_offset + 1) checking membership. If there's a slow/stuck earliest offset while new offsets keep being added, the all_offsets set grows unbounded (only cleaned up after commit at line 103), and each commit tick does O(n) work scanning the set plus O(range) iteration. This is a legitimate scalability concern for a production consumer, though it's not a correctness bug - the code will work correctly, just with degrading performance under sustained load with stuck offsets. The finding is grounded in actual diff code and represents a real architectural concern.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:202 — P2/100: `return hash(group_key) % self.num_queues` maps unrelated subscriptions onto one single-threaded FIFO, so any hot or slow subscription head-of-line blocks every colliding subscription and collapses usable parallelism; uniform hashing balances key counts but cannot balance per-key work or remove deterministic collisions.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a real architectural concern in the new code. The diff shows `get_queue_for_group` at line 202 uses `hash(group_key) % self.num_queues` to assign subscriptions to queues. With a fixed number of queues (default 20), multiple subscriptions will inevitably hash to the same queue. Since each queue has exactly one worker thread processing items in FIFO order (as documented in the FixedQueuePool docstring), a slow subscription will block all other subscriptions assigned to the same queue. This is a legitimate design tradeoff/concern rather than a bug - the code works as designed, but the design has head-of-line blocking implications that could affect performance. The finding is grounded in specific code from the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:31 — P2/100: `message: Message[KafkaPayload | FilteredPayload]` is never read after construction, so deleting this field and its constructor argument changes no behavior while preventing every unbounded backlog entry from retaining the original encoded Kafka payload alongside its decoded result; future offset access does not justify the coupling because `partition` and `offset` are already stored explicitly.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the `message` field in `WorkItem` is stored but never read after construction. Looking at the diff, `WorkItem` stores `message: Message[KafkaPayload | FilteredPayload]` (line 31), but examining all usages of `WorkItem` in the code - in `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` only `work_item.result`, `work_item.partition`, and `work_item.offset` are accessed. The `message` field is never used. This means each queued item retains the full Kafka payload unnecessarily, which could cause memory issues with large backlogs. This is a valid architectural concern about unnecessary memory retention, though not a bug since it doesn't cause incorrect behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:344 — P2/100: `def join(self, timeout: float | None = None) -> None: self.close()` ignores the `ProcessingStrategy.join` timeout contract and starts shutdown again, so a caller requesting a bounded join can instead wait through the commit-thread timeout plus up to five seconds for each worker.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the `join` method in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` (line 344) simply calls `self.close()` and ignores the `timeout` parameter. Looking at `close()` (lines 335-337), it sets the shutdown event, then calls `self.commit_thread.join(timeout=5.0)` and `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`. The `shutdown()` method (lines 224-232) joins each worker with `timeout=5.0`. This means `join(timeout=X)` will actually wait up to 5.0 seconds for the commit thread plus 5.0 seconds per worker, completely ignoring the caller's requested timeout. This violates the ProcessingStrategy interface contract where `join` should respect the provided timeout.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:233 — P1/100: `worker.shutdown = True` makes every worker exit after its current item before `shutdown(immediate=False)` can drain the queue, so a normal graceful close abandons all remaining uptime results despite the stated no-loss guarantee.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the shutdown() method in FixedQueuePool (lines 229-240), it first sets `worker.shutdown = True` for all workers, then calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` on queues. In OrderedQueueWorker.run() (lines 119-127), the worker checks `while not self.shutdown` and exits the loop when shutdown is True. This means workers will exit after processing their current item, before the queue's shutdown(immediate=False) can ensure all items are drained. The docstring claims 'No item is lost' but this shutdown sequence can abandon queued items.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:338 — P1/75: `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` destroys the factory-owned pool whenever an assignment strategy closes, so the next strategy created after a Kafka rebalance reuses queues with no live workers and cannot process its assigned messages.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real issue. Looking at the diff: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() at line 338 calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), and terminate() also calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(). The queue_pool is passed in from the factory (ResultsStrategyFactory) which owns it. In ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown() (line 182-184), it also calls self.queue_pool.shutdown() and sets it to None. However, the strategy's close/terminate methods are called during Kafka rebalances when the strategy is destroyed, but the factory persists. When close() is called on the strategy, it shuts down the factory's queue_pool. If a new strategy is created after rebalance via create_thread_queue_parallel_worker(), it reuses the same factory.queue_pool which has already been shut down (workers have shutdown=True and queues are shutdown). This is a real bug - the strategy shouldn't shutdown the factory-owned pool.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:185 — P1/100: `work_queue: queue.Queue[WorkItem[T]] = queue.Queue()` creates an unbounded queue per worker, so sustained input above processing capacity grows memory without limit instead of supplying the documented natural backpressure.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that queue.Queue() is created without a maxsize parameter at line 185, making it unbounded. The docstring for SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy at lines 237-244 explicitly claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' as a guarantee, but unbounded queues never fill up and thus cannot provide backpressure. This is a real defect where the implementation contradicts its documented behavior - sustained high input rates will cause unbounded memory growth rather than applying backpressure.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/result_consumer.py:136 — P2/100: `num_queues=max_workers or 20` accepts a negative `--max-workers` as a negative queue count and silently converts zero to 20, so validly parsed CLI inputs either create no usable workers or violate the requested parallelism limit.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `num_queues=max_workers or 20` at line 136. This code has two issues: (1) if max_workers is 0, the `or` operator treats it as falsy and uses 20 instead, which silently ignores the user's explicit setting; (2) if max_workers is negative, it passes through directly to FixedQueuePool. Looking at FixedQueuePool.__init__, it creates `range(num_queues)` queues - a negative value would create zero queues/workers, breaking the consumer. The CLI option at line 138 shows `type=int, default=None` with no validation for positive values, so negative integers are valid CLI inputs that would cause this bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py:1820 — P2/100: `assert mock_processor_call.call_count == 2` only proves both subscription callbacks eventually ran and passes when they run serially, leaving the feature's core cross-subscription parallelism requirement entirely unverified.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that test_thread_queue_parallel_concurrent_subscriptions at line 1820 only asserts mock_processor_call.call_count == 2, which verifies both messages were processed but doesn't actually verify they were processed concurrently/in parallel. The test name claims to test 'concurrent processing' but the assertion would pass even if messages were processed serially. This is a valid test coverage concern - the test doesn't verify the core parallelism feature it claims to test. However, this is not a bug in the production code, just an incomplete test that doesn't fully verify the concurrent behavior.

When `self.result_processor(self.identifier, work_item.result)` throws an exception (caught by `except Exception:` at line 141), the offset is still marked complete. adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:323 — P1/100: `self.queue_pool.offset_tracker.complete_offset(` unconditionally marks a record successful after any decode, grouping, or queue-submission exception, so schema-skewed records during rollout and records rejected by a closed pool are committed without processing; the strongest counterargument is that broad exception handling keeps consumption live, but it fails because liveness is purchased by irreversible silent loss with no quarantine or backfill source.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at lines 308-323 in queue_consumer.py, the exception handler catches any exception during decode/grouping/submission and then unconditionally marks the offset as complete via `add_offset` followed by `complete_offset`. This means if there's a schema error, grouping function failure, or queue submission failure, the message is marked as successfully processed and will be committed, resulting in silent data loss. adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/result_consumer.py:136 — P1/100: `num_queues=max_workers or 20` accepts a negative `--max-workers`, constructs no queues or workers, and makes every submission raise `IndexError` before the catch path marks its offset complete, silently committing unprocessed messages.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that negative max_workers would cause IndexError and silent message loss. However, examining the diff: 1) The CLI option at line 138 uses `type=int` with `default=None`, and click doesn't validate negative values by default, but 2) Looking at line 136: `num_queues=max_workers or 20` - if max_workers is negative (e.g., -1), it's truthy, so num_queues would be -1. However, `range(-1)` produces an empty iterator, so no queues/workers are created. 3) When submit() is called, `hash(group_key) % 0` would raise ZeroDivisionError (not IndexError). 4) The exception handler in submit() at lines 305-311 does mark the offset complete, but this is after an exception - the finding's claim about 'silently committing unprocessed messages' is partially valid but the mechanism described (IndexError) is wrong. More importantly, this is an edge case that requires intentional misuse (passing negative workers), and the diff doesn't introduce a regression - it's a new feature. The finding misidentifies the exception type and the practical likelihood is very low.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:338 — P1/75: `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` permanently closes the factory-owned shared pool when Arroyo closes one partition-assignment strategy, so the next `create_with_partitions` after a rebalance reuses shut queues whose rejected submissions are caught and marked complete without processing.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real issue: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` and `terminate()` (lines 337-343), `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` is called. The `queue_pool` is passed in from `ResultsStrategyFactory` which creates it once in `__init__` (lines 128-132) and stores it as `self.queue_pool`. When Arroyo calls `close()` on the strategy after a rebalance, the shared pool is shut down. The factory's `shutdown()` method (lines 180-183) also shuts down the pool and sets it to None, but the strategy's `close()` doesn't set it to None on the factory. On the next `create_with_partitions` call, `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker` (lines 241-254) asserts `self.queue_pool is not None` and reuses the already-shutdown pool. The `queue.Queue.shutdown()` causes subsequent `put()` calls to raise exceptions, which are caught in `submit()` (lines 295-302) and marked complete without processing.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:336 — P2/100: `self.shutdown_event.set()` stops the only commit loop before `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` waits for active workers, so work that finishes during close can never reach the commit callback and is replayed after restart.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the close() method in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy (lines 331-335), it first sets self.shutdown_event.set(), then joins the commit_thread, then calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(). The _commit_loop (lines 296-314) checks shutdown_event.is_set() to exit. The queue_pool.shutdown() (lines 227-237) sets worker.shutdown=True, calls q.shutdown(), and joins workers with timeout. The issue is: when close() is called, the commit loop stops immediately (shutdown_event.set()), but workers may still be processing items. When queue_pool.shutdown() waits for workers to finish (worker.join(timeout=5.0)), those workers complete work and call offset_tracker.complete_offset(), but the commit loop is already stopped and won't commit those offsets. This means work completed during shutdown won't have its offsets committed, causing replay on restart.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:234 — P2/100: `worker.shutdown = True` is set before non-immediate queue shutdown, so each worker exits after at most its current item and leaves all remaining queued messages abandoned instead of draining them during the advertised graceful shutdown.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the shutdown method in FixedQueuePool (lines 229-240), the code first sets `worker.shutdown = True` for all workers, then calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` on all queues. In the OrderedQueueWorker.run() method (lines 117-143), the worker checks `while not self.shutdown` before trying to get from the queue. When shutdown=True is set, workers will exit their loop after completing their current item, even though `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` is supposed to allow draining. The queue.ShutDown exception would only be raised after the queue is empty, but since workers check `self.shutdown` first, they exit before draining remaining items. This is a real bug where the graceful shutdown doesn't actually drain queued messages.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:149 — P1/100: `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset)` runs in `finally` after `except Exception:`, so a transient database or downstream failure is swallowed and its Kafka record becomes committable without being applied; skipping poison records is the strongest counterargument, but it fails because this catch treats retryable operational failures identically and preserves no replay or quarantine copy.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that in OrderedQueueWorker.run(), the finally block calls self.offset_tracker.complete_offset() regardless of whether processing succeeded or failed. When an exception occurs in result_processor(), it's caught by 'except Exception:', logged, but then the finally block still marks the offset as complete. This means failed messages will be committed as processed, causing data loss since they won't be reprocessed. The code at lines 140-149 shows: try block calls result_processor, except Exception logs the error, finally always calls complete_offset. This is a real correctness bug - transient failures should not result in the offset being marked complete.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:323 — P1/100: `self.queue_pool.offset_tracker.complete_offset(` marks a record complete after any decode, grouping, hashing, or queue-submission exception, so the commit loop permanently advances past work that never entered a worker; keeping the consumer live is the strongest counterargument, but it fails because logging alone cannot recover an already committed source record.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at lines 308-323 in queue_consumer.py, the submit() method has a try/except block where any exception during decoding, grouping, or queue submission causes the offset to be marked as both added and immediately completed. This means if there's an error processing a message (e.g., decoder throws, grouping_fn throws, or queue.put fails), the offset is marked complete without the work ever being processed by a worker. The commit loop in _commit_loop() will then commit this offset, permanently advancing past work that was never actually processed. This is a real bug - failed messages are silently skipped and their offsets committed, leading to data loss.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:301 — P1/100: `if result is None:` followed by `complete_offset(partition, offset)` converts the decoder's catch-all failure return into successful completion, so transient codec failures silently discard payloads; intentionally skipping `FilteredPayload` is the strongest counterargument, but it fails because `decode_payload` returns the same `None` for every unexpected decoding exception.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit(), when decoder returns None, the code immediately marks the offset as both added and completed (lines 299-302). Looking at decode_payload in result_consumer.py, it catches exceptions and returns None for decoding failures (not just FilteredPayload). This means transient decoding errors would silently skip messages rather than failing or retrying. The diff shows decode_payload returns None on exception (line 188-189 in result_consumer.py shows the pattern), and the submit method treats all None returns identically by completing the offset. This is a real correctness issue where failed decodes are silently dropped.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:336 — P1/100: `self.shutdown_event.set()` stops the sole commit loop before `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` sets every `worker.shutdown = True`, so graceful close abandons queued results and returns while results finishing after the final commit snapshot remain uncommitted and replay; eventual Kafka replay is the strongest counterargument, but it fails because the advertised graceful operation is partial and re-executes side effects already completed during shutdown.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the close() method in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy (lines 336-339), it calls self.shutdown_event.set() first, which stops the commit loop thread, then calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(). The commit loop in _commit_loop() (lines 278-296) checks shutdown_event.is_set() to exit. The issue is that when close() is called, the commit thread stops immediately, but workers may still be processing items. The queue_pool.shutdown() then sets worker.shutdown=True and calls queue.shutdown(), but any items that complete processing after the commit loop has exited will have their offsets marked complete via offset_tracker.complete_offset() but never committed. This is a real race condition - the commit loop exits before all workers finish, so final offset commits are lost. While Kafka replay would re-process these messages, this violates the 'graceful shutdown' semantics and causes duplicate processing of already-completed work.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/result_consumer.py:133 — P1/75: `self.queue_pool = FixedQueuePool(` creates one factory-owned pool while each assignment strategy executes `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` in `close()`, so the next `create_with_partitions` after a rebalance reuses shut queues whose rejected submissions are caught and committed as complete; final factory cleanup is the strongest counterargument, but it fails because assignment strategies close during rebalances while the factory remains reusable.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real issue: FixedQueuePool is created once in __init__ when mode='thread-queue-parallel' (line 133), but SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() calls self.queue_pool.shutdown() (line 340). After a rebalance, create_with_partitions would be called again, but the queue_pool has already been shut down. Looking at the shutdown method in FixedQueuePool (lines 227-237), it sets worker.shutdown=True and calls q.shutdown() on all queues. The factory's shutdown() method (lines 180-183) also shuts down the queue_pool and sets it to None. However, the strategy's close() method calls self.queue_pool.shutdown() directly, which would shut down the shared pool. This is a legitimate concern - if a rebalance occurs and close() is called on the strategy, the pool gets shut down, but the factory might try to create a new strategy with the same (now shut down) pool.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:185 — P1/100: `work_queue: queue.Queue[WorkItem[T]] = queue.Queue()` gives every worker an unbounded queue, so Kafka input above processing capacity grows retained payloads and decoded results until OOM instead of applying backpressure; bounded Kafka polling is the strongest counterargument, but it fails because every `submit()` returns immediately regardless of downstream backlog.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that in FixedQueuePool.__init__ (lines 175-185), each queue is created as `queue.Queue()` without a maxsize parameter, making them unbounded. The submit() method (lines 197-203) calls `work_queue.put(work_item)` which will never block on an unbounded queue. This means if messages arrive faster than workers can process them, the queues will grow indefinitely, holding decoded results in memory. While Kafka consumer polling could theoretically provide backpressure, the SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() method (lines 268-298) immediately puts items into queues without any blocking mechanism, so there's no backpressure propagation back to Kafka. This is a legitimate memory safety concern for a production consumer.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/result_consumer.py:136 — P1/100: `num_queues=max_workers or 20` accepts a negative parsed `--max-workers`, constructs zero queues, and causes every submission to raise before the broad catch marks its offset complete, silently committing the entire unprocessed stream; invalid operator input is the strongest counterargument, but it fails because the CLI accepts the value and the runtime reports successful consumption instead of rejecting startup.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real issue: when max_workers is negative (e.g., -1), `max_workers or 20` evaluates to -1 (truthy), and `FixedQueuePool` is created with `num_queues=-1`. Looking at the FixedQueuePool.__init__ in the diff (lines 163-185), `for i in range(num_queues)` with num_queues=-1 creates zero queues and zero workers. When submit() is called, `hash(group_key) % self.num_queues` would cause a ZeroDivisionError (or modulo by -1 gives unexpected results). However, the exception handling in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() (lines 296-306) catches all exceptions and marks offsets complete, which would silently commit without processing. The CLI does accept negative integers since click.Option with type=int doesn't validate for positive values. This is a legitimate edge case bug where invalid input leads to silent data loss.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:281 — P3/100: `metrics.incr("remote_subscriptions.queue_pool.offsets_committed",` executes before `self.commit_function(committable)`, so every failed commit is reported as committed and the same offsets inflate the success counter on each retry; eventual retry success is the strongest counterargument, but it fails because monitoring lies throughout the outage and overcounts the final successful offsets.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the _commit_loop method in queue_consumer.py lines 275-292, the code first calls metrics.incr() at line 281 to record offsets as committed, then calls self.commit_function(committable) at line 287. If commit_function raises an exception, the metrics have already been incremented but the commit failed. The exception is caught at line 290 and logged, but the metrics are not rolled back. On the next iteration, the same offsets would be retrieved again (since mark_committed wasn't called) and metrics.incr would be called again, inflating the counter. This is a real ordering bug where metrics are recorded before the actual commit succeeds.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:185 — P2, confidence 75: `work_queue: queue.Queue[WorkItem[T]] = queue.Queue()` creates an unbounded per-worker queue, so a result flood or hot subscription that lets Kafka delivery outpace processing grows resident memory until the uptime consumer is killed and results stop being processed; Kafka-side pacing is the strongest counterargument, but it does not survive because `submit()` has no capacity check or blocking boundary and `Queue`'s default `maxsize=0` never backpressures.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that queue.Queue() is created with default maxsize=0 (unbounded) at line 185 in the diff. The submit() method at line 199 calls work_queue.put() without any capacity check. This is a legitimate architectural concern - if processing is slower than message arrival, memory will grow unboundedly. However, this is not strictly a bug since the code will function correctly under normal load; it's a design concern about backpressure handling. The finding is grounded in actual diff code and raises a valid scalability/reliability concern for the new thread-queue-parallel mode.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py:1922 — (P1, confidence 100) `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` samples state only 0.2 seconds after work finishes even though the commit loop runs once per second, so it passes while the failed offset is marked complete and later committed, causing message loss; the strongest counterargument is that the test only needs to prove the second message runs, but its claimed error-handling contract is specifically about commits and the assertion never observes the commit interval.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a timing issue in the test. Looking at the diff, the test `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` at line 1922 asserts `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` after waiting only 0.2 seconds (`time.sleep(0.2)`) after processing completes. However, the commit loop in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop` (lines 268-286) runs with `self.shutdown_event.wait(1.0)`, meaning it commits once per second. The test's assertion samples state before the commit loop has a chance to run, so it may pass even though the failed offset gets marked complete (via `complete_offset` in the exception handler at lines 143-145 of `OrderedQueueWorker.run`) and would be committed on the next commit cycle. This is a real test bug - the test claims to verify error handling prevents commits but doesn't wait long enough to actually observe the commit behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py:2005 — (P1, confidence 100) `assert factory.queue_pool is None` proves only that a reference was cleared, so the graceful-shutdown test passes when queued results are dropped or the strategy's commit thread remains alive; the strongest counterargument is that `shutdown()` joins workers, but the assertion never verifies all five submitted results were processed or that the strategy thread terminated.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the test `test_thread_queue_parallel_graceful_shutdown` at line 2005 only asserts `factory.queue_pool is None` after calling `shutdown()`. Looking at the diff, the test submits 5 results but never verifies they were processed before shutdown. The `shutdown()` method in `FixedQueuePool` (lines 227-237) sets worker.shutdown=True and calls queue.shutdown(), but the test doesn't verify the 5 submitted items were actually processed. This is a legitimate test quality concern - the test claims to verify 'graceful shutdown' but doesn't actually verify that queued work completed. However, this is a test coverage gap, not a bug in the production code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py:1820 — (P2, confidence 100) `assert mock_processor_call.call_count == 2` proves completion rather than concurrency, so a fully serial implementation or two subscription IDs hashing to the same queue passes and the parallelism feature can regress undetected; the strongest counterargument is that two workers were configured, but no barrier, overlap interval, or worker identity is asserted.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that test_thread_queue_parallel_concurrent_subscriptions only asserts mock_processor_call.call_count == 2, which proves both messages were processed but doesn't verify they were processed concurrently. The test creates 2 subscriptions and sends 2 messages with max_workers=2, but a serial implementation would also pass this test. The finding is valid - this is a test that doesn't actually verify the concurrency feature it claims to test. However, this is not a bug in the production code, but rather an incomplete test for the new thread-queue-parallel feature.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py:200 — (P3, confidence 100) `assert stats["total_items"] > 0` races live workers running a trivial processor and fails whenever they drain all ten queues before the snapshot; the strongest counterargument is that ten submissions usually create a backlog, but queue size excludes in-flight work and scheduling can deterministically make the observed total zero.

adjudication.rationale: The test at line 200 submits 10 items to a FixedQueuePool with 3 queues and worker threads, then immediately calls get_stats() and asserts total_items > 0. However, the worker threads are daemon threads that start immediately upon pool creation and begin processing items as soon as they're submitted. Since the result_processor is trivial (just appending to a list), the workers can drain all queues before the assertion executes. The assertion is racy - it assumes items will still be queued when checked, but there's no synchronization to guarantee this. The test does wait for completion afterward, but the intermediate assertion on queue depth is fundamentally flaky.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py:106 — (P3, confidence 100) `assert len(queue_indices) == 3` assumes salted Python hashes for twenty fixed strings occupy every bucket and fails under `PYTHONHASHSEED=211`, where they occupy only two; the strongest counterargument is that twenty samples make full coverage likely, but randomized test-process seeds turn that probability into reproducible CI flakiness.

adjudication.rationale: The test at line 106 creates 20 groups ('group0' through 'group19') and asserts they distribute across all 3 queues. The hash distribution depends on Python's string hashing, which is randomized by PYTHONHASHSEED in test environments. With only 20 samples and 3 buckets, there's a non-trivial probability that not all 3 buckets will be hit with certain hash seeds. The finding correctly identifies this as a flaky test - the assertion `assert len(queue_indices) == 3` can fail when the hash function happens to map all 20 strings to only 2 of the 3 buckets. This is a real bug in the test code introduced by this diff.
